title: Northrop Grumman Beats Earnings Estimates but Stock Slides on Margin Concerns
excerpt: The defense giant posted Q2 EPS of $7.68, well above the $6.82 consensus, and raised its full-year outlook, but operating income declines in two key segments sent shares to a new 52-week low.
body:
Key Takeaways
  • Northrop Grumman's Q2 EPS of $7.68 surpassed estimates, but stock fell 2.3% to a 52-week low.
  • Full-year 2026 EPS guidance raised to $28.60–$29.10, with sales outlook increased to $43.75–$44.25 billion.
  • Total backlog reached a record $104.7 billion, boosted by $20 billion in net awards this quarter.
  • Operating income declined 38% in defense systems and 16% in space systems, raising margin concerns.

  • Northrop Grumman reported Q2 earnings of $7.68 per share on revenue of $10.88 billion, beating Wall Street estimates of $6.82 EPS and $10.81 billion in sales.
  • The company raised its full-year 2026 adjusted EPS guidance to $28.60–$29.10, up from $27.40–$27.90, and lifted its sales outlook to $43.75–$44.25 billion.
  • Total backlog surged 9% to a record $104.7 billion, driven by $20 billion in net awards during the quarter.
  • Shares fell 2.3% to $512.29 as operating income dropped 38% in the defense systems segment and 16% in space systems, with analysts flagging the earnings beat as largely tax-driven.

A Beat-and-Raise Quarter Meets a Skeptical Market

Northrop Grumman delivered a second-quarter earnings beat that looked strong on the surface but failed to convince investors. The Falls Church, Virginia-based defense contractor reported earnings of $7.68 per share on revenue of $10.88 billion for the three months ended June 30, comfortably topping analyst expectations of $6.82 EPS and $10.81 billion in revenue, according to FactSet.

The company also raised its full-year 2026 guidance, now projecting adjusted earnings of $28.60 to $29.10 per share, up from the $27.40 to $27.90 range issued in April. Sales guidance was lifted by a quarter-billion dollars to $43.75 billion to $44.25 billion. Wall Street had been projecting $27.94 in full-year EPS before the update.

None of it was enough. Shares dropped 2.3% on Tuesday to close at $512.29, hitting a new 52-week low, even as the broader S&P 500 gained 0.9%. The stock is now down roughly 8% year to date and about 28% from recent highs.

Tax Tailwind, Not Operational Strength

> **"Shares dropped 2.3% on Tuesday to close at $512.29, hitting a new 52-week low, even as the broader S&P 500 gained 0.9%."**

Analysts were quick to note that the headline earnings beat was driven primarily by a sharp drop in Northrop's effective tax rate — to about 6% from 18% a year earlier — rather than by improved operations. CFO John Greene confirmed the tax benefit on the earnings call.

"We expect the stock to underperform on this result."

— Matt Akers, Analyst, BNP Paribas

Operating profit of $1.1 billion came in roughly in line with estimates, but the segment-level picture was less encouraging. Operating income in Northrop's defense systems unit fell 38% year-over-year, while its space systems segment saw a 16% decline. The defense systems hit stemmed from higher-than-expected costs to develop the Stand-in Attack Weapon air-to-surface missile and to scale production of the extended-range Advanced Anti-Radiation Guided Missile. In the space segment, increased projected costs to complete the GEM 63XL rocket booster program — following a launch anomaly earlier this year — weighed on margins.

B-21 Raider Drives Aeronautics Growth

The brightest spot was aeronautics, Northrop's largest revenue segment, where sales climbed 13% driven by the B-21 Raider stealth bomber program and other classified work. In February, Northrop signed an Air Force agreement expanding B-21 production capacity by 25%, with the first delivery set for 2027.

Record Backlog Growth
›Total backlog surged 9% to $104.7 billion.
›$20 billion in net awards during the quarter.
›Strong long-term revenue visibility.
Northrop Grumman earnings report

"With the recent agreements on B-21 and the strong sales results in 2Q26, we believe the guide could be conservative."

— Herbert Ken, Analyst, RBC

Total sales rose 5% across all four divisions — aeronautics, defense systems, mission systems, and space systems. Net awards of $20 billion during the quarter pushed the total backlog to a record $104.7 billion, providing strong long-term revenue visibility.

Defense Stocks Under Broader Pressure

Northrop's post-earnings decline fits a wider pattern across the defense sector. Despite surging demand driven by the wars in Ukraine and the Middle East — the Pentagon estimates the U.S. has expended more than 50,000 rockets, missiles, and other projectiles since 2022 — defense stocks have broadly underperformed this year. President Trump has pushed contractors to expand manufacturing capacity, but investors are pricing in risks around potential defense budget pressure if Democrats gain ground in upcoming midterm elections, according to Barron's.

JP Morgan analyst Seth Seifman noted that expectations heading into the quarter were not particularly high: "Given the market's tendency to punish execution challenges, we could see pressure on the stock."

What to Watch

For investors, the key question is whether Northrop can translate its record backlog into improved operational execution. The company said it expects to begin delivering redesigned GEM 63XL rocket motors by year-end, which could help ease margin pressure in the space segment. The B-21 production ramp remains a potential catalyst heading into 2027. But until margins improve and the tax-adjusted earnings picture clears up, the stock may continue to struggle for direction despite strong top-line growth.
